newsitem.title: INDIA: WEEKAHEAD-Bargains seen in volatile India shares.
newsitem.headline: WEEKAHEAD-Bargains seen in volatile India shares.

text.p: Foreign funds are expected to shrug off lethargy and look at bargain opportunities in volatile Indian shares this week, traders and analysts said.

They said political instability worries had waned with the resignation of a powerful politician involved in a corruption scandal, and players would look to fundamental factors like easier liquidity and economic revival hopes.
A government statement on Saturday said India's index of industrial production rose by 9.8 percent in April compared with the same month in 1996.

"I am optimistic. There is no new political factor to cause distress," said Nirmal Jain, managing director at Probity Research & Financial Services, an investment consultancy firm that serves foreign and local institutions.
"One big uncertainty factor is over. We should see foreign fund money pushing up stocks."

The Bombay Stock Exchange's (BSE) benchmark index last week rose 65 points, or nearly two percent, to end at 4,189.81 after posting the year's biggest weekly fall of five percent in the previous week.
India's United Front coalition late on Friday said it had decided not to admit in its fold a breakaway group headed by the scandal-tainted leader Laloo Prasad Yadav.

Yadav resigned as chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar earlier on Friday after an agonising debate on corruption which had unsettled Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's 15-party coalition and derailed a bull run in Indian stocks.
Neeraj Batra, president of Hinduja Finance, said markets had more-or-less discounted the worst of Indian politics.
"Markets have a lot of reasons to go up such as rising liquidity and overseas buying," Batra told Reuters.
Falling interest rates, abundant liquidity and expectations of an economic upturn that had fuelled a 36 percent bull run in the share index stood unchanged, traders said.

"As interest rates continue to ease, liquidity improves and government policies remain positive for business, we expect selected stocks to continue to be rerated," investment banker Morgan Stanley Dean Witter said in a mid-July report.
It said the weakness in shares induced by political uncertainty must be seen as a buy opportunity.
Some brokers expect the market to trade within a tight range this week as participants awaiting direction.
"There is a little bit of uncertainty on whether the government can cope with its problems," said Ajit Sanghvi, a member-broker of the BSE.
"But, any big crack in the (Bombay) index is likely to be its bottom level."
The market will also be on the look-out for clearer signs of an economic revival forecast by many analysts, brokers said.

"...despite some deceleration in growth in 1996/97, the current economic scene reveals several positive trends, which would accelerate the growth momentum in 1997/98," Reserve Bank of India governer Chakravarty Rangarajan told a meeting with business leaders last week.
India's gross domestic product (GDP) growth slowed to 6.8 percent in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) from 7.1 percent the year before.

Rangarajan said increased deposits, falling interest rates, major tax incentives in this year's budget and better prospects for export growth would lead to "much better growth performance in 1997/98".
